analysis.one_liner: Strips qualified immunity so victims can sue police officers for violating their rights.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in January 2026 with 14 Democratic cosponsors and referred to the House Judiciary Committee, which has taken no action on it since.
analysis.plain_summary: When a police officer violates someone's constitutional rights, a judge-built doctrine called qualified immunity usually blocks the lawsuit unless the victim can show a prior court case made that exact violation clearly illegal. This bill writes qualified immunity out of the main federal civil rights statute, so officers can no longer use the good-faith or not-clearly-established defenses in civil suits. It also opens federal law enforcement officers acting under federal authority to those same lawsuits for the first time, and applies to cases already pending or filed after enactment.
analysis.who_benefits: People whose constitutional rights are violated by federal, state, or local law enforcement. Under current doctrine, many such cases are thrown out before a jury ever hears them because the victim cannot point to an earlier case with nearly identical facts. The bill would let those cases reach a jury, and it applies to suits already in court when it becomes law [S2].

how_it_helps.text: The bill adds a subsection to the civil rights statute (42 U.S.C. 1983) barring four classic qualified immunity defenses: good faith, a reasonable or unreasonable belief the conduct was lawful, rights not clearly established, and unclear law at the time of the violation [S2].
It applies to actions pending on or filed after enactment, so people whose suits were already filed would benefit, not only future victims [S2].
It extends the statute to federal law enforcement officers acting under federal authority, closing a gap in which victims of federal officers often had no equivalent suit [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Law enforcement officers would face personal civil liability in cases where they would currently be shielded, and state and local governments, along with their insurers and ultimately taxpayers, would bear more lawsuits and payouts. Police departments and unions argue this could make split-second decisions riskier for officers and chill proactive policing, and some warn of difficulty recruiting and keeping officers.
analysis.who_pays_short: Officers and local governments' liability costs

drawbacks.text: The bill does not create a narrower alternative such as shifting liability to the employer; it leaves individual officers personally exposed, which police groups and some courts warn could deter aggressive policing or make recruitment harder [S2].

Taxpayers and municipal budgets would absorb more lawsuit judgments and insurance costs, and officers themselves would face financially ruinous suits even for honest mistakes, since the bill bars even a reasonable good-faith belief defense [S2].
The bill applies retroactively to suits already pending, which courts and opponents typically criticize as changing the rules mid-case [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The gain is real and concrete: victims of rights violations would finally get their day in court instead of losing at the summary-judgment stage to the clearly-established rule. The cost is borne by officers individually and by local government budgets, and the bill does nothing to route liability toward departments that set policy, which is the reform many scholars prefer. Whether the deterrent benefit to the public outweighs the chilling effect on policing is a genuine judgment call, and the bill takes the strong version of the reform rather than a compromise.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee has not held a hearing or taken any action since.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on January 13, 2026, by Rep. Ayanna Pressley with Reps. Omar and Simon, and referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary [S1][S2][S4].
Fourteen House Democrats have cosponsored it; no Republican has [S3].
The full action history shows only introduction, referral, and the sponsor's introductory remarks, with no hearing, markup, or floor action [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Law enforcement officers and their unions keep qualified immunity as a shield, and local governments avoid expanded liability costs; victims of police misconduct remain without the legal remedy the bill offered.

for.name: Rep. Ayanna Pressley
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the House floor.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and has not scheduled a hearing or markup in the months since.

against.name: 223 of 223 House Republicans
against.what_they_did: No House Republican cosponsored the bill.

sides.party_line_note: All 15 sponsors and cosponsors are Democrats and no Republican has signed on, but no vote has been taken, so the partisan split on the merits is inferred from sponsorship rather than roll calls.

industries.note: Qualified immunity is the doctrine that shields officers from civil suits for constitutional violations; abolishing it exposes officers to personal liability. The industry's interest in keeping the shield runs directly against the public's ability to obtain a remedy.
Unions representing officers defend qualified immunity as protection for members making split-second decisions; their members would face suits they currently cannot be sued in.

industries.industry: Municipal governments and their liability insurers
industries.note: Cities and counties would face more civil rights judgments and higher insurance costs, costs that often fall on taxpayers; though some municipalities also benefit when departments are held accountable for misconduct.

analysis.trajectory: With no Republican cosponsors, only 14 of 217 House Democrats behind it, and no committee action months after referral, the realistic path is that the bill sits in the Judiciary Committee and expires at the end of this Congress without a hearing or vote, as prior versions of qualified-immunity repeal have. It could advance only if Democratic leadership prioritizes a police-reform package, which this bill's early reception gives no sign of.
